title: Scandinavian: each side's setup and what each move prepares
outcomes: Names, for each early move of the model setup, what it does now and what it makes possible later
Shows which earlier moves emptied the squares that make long castling legal
Explains why Black prepares ...c6 and ...Nf6 before the bishop and pawn moves
Recognises a move-order switch that reaches the same setup
Shows how ...e6 and ...Be7 prepare Black's short castling

steps.chapter: A setup is a list of jobs

steps.prompt: Pick one move by each side that you think made the rest of this setup possible, and say why.

fields.label: My two moves and my reason:

steps.text: **The question of this lesson.** In a good setup every early move does two jobs: something now, and something it makes possible later. We walk one model setup, whose moves the engine rates within about 0.4 pawns of its first choice at depth 16 [V], not a book line. For each move, ask what it prepares. By the end you can name the job of each move on both sides, and say what changes with a different move order.

line.say: The pawn takes the centre, controls c5 and e5, and opens the diagonal of the c1 bishop.

After 4.d4 the pawn attacks e5.

The squares between king and rook are empty because b1, c1 and d1 were each emptied earlier. White castles long.

steps.title: One empty square makes the difference
steps.prompt: May White castle queenside? Predict each, then check.

steps.text: **Reading the payoff.** Ask three questions of any early move: which squares did it empty, which squares does it control or attack, and which move is now legal that was not before? Castling long needed three empty squares, and three different earlier moves emptied them one by one. [I] Nobody has to plan all three at once; each is a sensible move for its own reasons, and together they pay off.

line.say: The knight develops and watches e4 and d5, so a White piece cannot settle on e4 easily.

steps.chapter: Black's moves and what each prepares

steps.caption: Black to move. Step through the pawn move and the bishop move it supports.

line.say: The pawn covers b5 and d5 and opens c7.
White develops the bishop.
The bishop comes out before any pawn blocks it, and it hits the pawn on c2.

claims.statement: After ...c6 one black pawn attacks b5.
After ...Bf5 one black piece attacks c2.
No white piece is loose, so the pawn on c2 is defended.

steps.text: **Why this order.** [I] ...Nf6 develops and watches e4 and d5. ...c6 covers b5 and d5 and empties c7, so the queen has a retreat. The bishop leaves before ...e6 because ...e6 would shut it in. Then the b8 knight comes to d7, and ...e6 frees the king's bishop, as the next board shows. Each move is small, and each answers one question: what is still undone?

steps.caption: Black to move. Step through the pawn move that opens the king's bishop, and the way the outside bishop survives a knight attack.

line.say: The pawn opens the diagonal of the f8 bishop and guards f5 and d5.
White attacks the bishop on f5.
The bishop steps back along the same diagonal and stays outside the pawn chain.

claims.statement: Before ...e6 the bishop on f8 has no legal move.
After ...e6 the bishop on f8 has 5 legal moves.
At the end the engine (depth 16) rates the position between 0.2 and 1.1 pawns for White.

steps.caption: Black to move. ...e6 prepares more than the bishop: step through Black's own castling.

line.say: The bishop steps out of the way. f8 and g8 are now empty, so Black can castle short.
White brings a rook to the e-file.
Black castles. The king is safe behind the pawns on f7, g7 and h7, and the rook comes to f8.

claims.statement: After the castling the black king stands on g8.
After the castling a black rook stands on f8.

steps.text: **Move orders.** After the queen takes on d5, White chose the knight to c3 in 1,275 master games and the knight to f3 in 122 (our data). Online the counts are 101,222 and 16,438. The c3 knight forces the queen to move at once. The f3 knight does not attack it, so Black can develop first; online, the bishop to g4 was Black's most common reply (4,969 games). [V] Counts of games. The next board compares the engine's view and shows that the two move orders can meet.

steps.prompt: Teach it back. For a beginner, name two moves of the setup for each side, say what each does now and what it makes possible later, and name one move-order choice.

fields.label: One example a beginner could set up on a board:

steps.text: **Self-check.** For each of four moves, did you say what it does now and what it makes possible? Did you name the three squares that had to be emptied for long castling? Did you say why ...e6 waits until the bishop is out? Could you set up the move-order switch on a board for a friend? Did you name one mistake?

**What to remember.** Ask of every move: what does it empty, what does it control, what is now legal? The d-pawn opens a bishop and takes squares. The knight guards it. The bishop, queen and knight moves empty the squares for castling long. Black's pawn on c6 and knight on f6 give the queen a home; the bishop comes out before ...e6. Move orders can meet. The setup is a model, not a rule.
